questions.s: Which concept treats a business as separate from its owner, so the owner's private house is not shown in the business's books?
questions.e: The business entity concept keeps the owner's private affairs out of the business records; only business transactions are recorded. Going concern is about the business continuing, not about separating owner and firm.

questions.s: A plot bought for Rs 2,000,000 is now worth Rs 3,500,000 but is still shown in the books at Rs 2,000,000. Which concept explains this?
questions.e: Under the historical cost concept, assets are recorded at what was paid for them, not at current market value. Realisation concerns when revenue is recognised, not how assets are valued.

questions.s: The going concern concept is the main reason why accountants:
o: record sales when cash is finally received
keep the owner's drawings in a separate account
use one depreciation method year after year
show fixed assets at cost less depreciation
questions.e: Because the business is expected to keep operating, fixed assets are shown at cost less depreciation rather than at what they would fetch in a forced sale. Using the same method each year is the consistency concept.

questions.s: A business has assets of Rs 500,000 and liabilities of Rs 180,000. What is the owner's capital?
questions.e: Capital = Assets − Liabilities = Rs 500,000 − Rs 180,000 = Rs 320,000. Adding the two (Rs 680,000) forgets that liabilities are claims of outsiders, not of the owner.

questions.s: Bilal starts a business with cash of Rs 400,000, buys furniture on credit for Rs 60,000 and withdraws Rs 15,000 cash for personal use. What are the total assets of the business?
questions.e: Cash 400,000 − 15,000 = 385,000, plus furniture 60,000, gives total assets of Rs 445,000. Rs 460,000 ignores that drawings take cash out of the business.

questions.s: Goods are bought for cash. What is the effect on the accounting equation?
o: One asset rises and another falls by the same amount
Assets and capital both rise by the same amount
Assets and liabilities both fall by the same amount
Assets and liabilities both rise by the same amount
questions.e: Stock (an asset) rises and cash (another asset) falls, so the totals do not change. Liabilities would rise only if the goods were bought on credit.

questions.s: A business pays a creditor Rs 20,000 by cheque. What is the effect on the accounting equation?
o: Assets fall by Rs 20,000 and capital falls by Rs 20,000
Liabilities fall by Rs 20,000 and capital rises by Rs 20,000
Assets fall by Rs 20,000 and liabilities fall by Rs 20,000
Assets rise by Rs 20,000 and liabilities fall by Rs 20,000
questions.e: The bank balance (an asset) goes down and the amount owed to the creditor (a liability) goes down by the same amount. Capital is not affected, because paying a debt is not an expense.

questions.s: Which of the following accounts normally has a debit balance?
questions.e: Drawings reduce the owner's capital, so they are recorded on the debit side and carry a debit balance. Capital, creditors and sales all increase on the credit side.

questions.s: Ayesha's shop receives Rs 12,000 in cash as rent for letting out part of its premises. Which entry is correct?
questions.e: Cash comes in, so Cash is debited; rent received is an income, and incomes increase with a credit. Crediting Capital would wrongly treat business income as money introduced by the owner.

questions.s: Which source document is used to record a credit purchase of goods in the buyer's books?
o: Credit note received from the supplier
Cash memo issued to a customer
questions.e: The supplier's invoice shows the goods, prices and amount owed, and is the basis for entering a credit purchase. A credit note records a reduction, such as for goods returned.

questions.s: When a buyer returns goods to the seller, which document does the buyer usually send with them?
questions.e: The buyer sends a debit note, showing that the supplier's account is being debited for the returned goods. The seller replies with a credit note.

questions.s: Ahmed Traders issue a credit note of Rs 4,000 to a customer, Zain, for goods returned. How is Zain's account affected in Ahmed Traders' books?
questions.e: Zain now owes Rs 4,000 less, so his account (an asset, a debtor) is credited; Returns Inwards is debited. Debiting him would increase what he owes.

questions.s: Under the prudence concept, closing stock is valued at:
o: the higher of cost and net realisable value
its current selling price in every case
the lower of cost and net realisable value
its cost even if it can only be sold for less
questions.e: Prudence means losses are recognised as soon as they are expected, so stock is written down when it can be sold for less than cost. Using the higher value would anticipate a profit not yet earned.

questions.s: December's salary of Rs 45,000 is unpaid at the year end of 31 December but is still charged in that year's income statement. Which concept requires this?
questions.e: The matching concept charges expenses in the period in which they help earn revenue, whether or not cash has been paid. Realisation is about when revenue, not expense, is recognised.

questions.s: A customer orders goods in March, receives them in April and pays for them in May. Under the realisation concept, in which month is the sale recorded?
o: Half in April, half in May
questions.e: Revenue is realised when goods are delivered and the buyer becomes liable to pay, which happens in April. An order alone creates no sale, and the date of payment does not decide when the sale is recorded.

questions.s: Because of the money measurement concept, which of the following is NOT recorded in a shop's books?
o: A loan received from a bank
The loyalty and skill of the shop's staff
Wages paid to the shop's staff
Goods taken by the owner for home use
questions.e: Only items that can be measured in money are recorded. Staff loyalty may be valuable but has no reliable money value; the other three are all money transactions.

questions.s: A firm uses the straight-line method of depreciation one year, the reducing balance method the next year, and switches back again the year after. Which concept does this break?
questions.e: Consistency requires the same accounting methods to be used from year to year, so results can be compared. Switching methods without good reason makes profits of different years incomparable.

questions.s: A stapler costing Rs 400 will last for several years, yet the business writes it off as an expense in the year of purchase. Which concept allows this?
questions.e: Under materiality, items too small to affect a reader's decisions need not be treated strictly; depreciating a Rs 400 stapler over years would cost more effort than it is worth. Historical cost concerns valuation, not this simplification.

questions.s: Which concept is the basis of the double-entry system of book-keeping?
questions.e: The dual aspect concept says every transaction has two equal effects, one debit and one credit, which is exactly what double entry records. The other concepts do not concern the two-sidedness of transactions.

questions.s: Usman brings his personal car, valued at Rs 900,000, into the business for business use. Which entry is made in the business's books?
questions.e: The business gains an asset (Vehicles, debit) and the owner's investment rises (Capital, credit). No cash is paid, and it is not a loan because the owner is investing in his own business.

questions.s: The owner takes goods costing Rs 5,000 from the shop for household use. Which entry is correct?
questions.e: Goods withdrawn are drawings, and Purchases is credited at cost to remove them from the goods available for sale. Crediting Sales would wrongly record a profit on goods the owner simply took.

questions.s: A trader's capital at the start of the year was Rs 250,000. During the year he made a net profit of Rs 60,000, withdrew Rs 24,000 and introduced further capital of Rs 30,000. What was his capital at the end of the year?
questions.e: Closing capital = 250,000 + 60,000 − 24,000 + 30,000 = Rs 316,000. Rs 286,000 leaves out the extra capital introduced; Rs 340,000 forgets to deduct the drawings.

questions.s: A trader's capital at the end of the year was Rs 420,000. Her net profit for the year was Rs 75,000 and her drawings were Rs 30,000. No new capital was introduced. What was her capital at the start of the year?
questions.e: Closing = Opening + Profit − Drawings, so Opening = 420,000 − 75,000 + 30,000 = Rs 375,000. Rs 315,000 deducts drawings again instead of adding them back.

questions.s: In accounting, who are 'debtors'?
o: Suppliers to whom the business owes money
Banks that have lent money to the business
Customers who owe money to the business
questions.e: Debtors (trade receivables) are people who have bought on credit and still owe the business; they are assets. Suppliers owed money are creditors, a liability.

questions.s: Goods costing Rs 30,000 are sold on credit for Rs 40,000. What is the overall effect on the accounting equation?
o: Assets rise by Rs 40,000 and liabilities rise by Rs 40,000
Assets stay the same and capital rises by Rs 10,000
Assets rise by Rs 10,000 and capital rises by Rs 10,000
Assets rise by Rs 40,000 and capital rises by Rs 40,000
questions.e: Debtors rise by 40,000 and stock falls by 30,000, a net rise in assets of 10,000; the 10,000 profit increases capital. The whole 40,000 is not added because stock costing 30,000 has gone out.

questions.s: At the start of a year a business had assets of Rs 700,000 and liabilities of Rs 200,000. At the end of the year its assets were Rs 850,000 and liabilities Rs 230,000. The owner withdrew Rs 40,000 and introduced no new capital. What was the profit for the year?
questions.e: Opening capital = 500,000 and closing capital = 620,000, an increase of 120,000. Drawings reduced capital, so profit = 120,000 + 40,000 = Rs 160,000. Rs 150,000 looks only at assets and ignores the change in liabilities.

questions.s: Why does the owner's capital account normally show a credit balance?
o: Capital is an asset owned by the business
Capital is an income earned by the business
The business owes this amount to the owner
The owner owes this amount to the business
questions.e: Under the entity concept the business is separate from its owner, so capital is a claim of the owner on the business, like a liability, and sits on the credit side. It is neither an asset nor an income.

questions.s: Under the traditional classification of accounts, the Salaries account is a:
questions.e: Salaries is an expense, and expenses and incomes are nominal accounts. Outstanding Salaries, the amount still owed to staff, would be a representative personal account.

questions.s: Under the traditional classification of accounts, the Goodwill account is a:
o: real account of an intangible asset
questions.e: Goodwill is an asset without physical form, so it is an intangible real account. An artificial personal account is one for a firm or institution, such as a bank.

questions.s: Goods are sold on credit to Kamran. By the rule for personal accounts, Kamran's account is debited because he is:
questions.e: The rule for personal accounts is 'debit the receiver, credit the giver'. Kamran receives the goods, so he is debited. 'What goes out' belongs to the rule for real accounts.

questions.s: Furniture is bought for cash. How does the rule for real accounts apply?
o: Furniture comes in and is debited; Cash goes out and is credited
Furniture comes in and is credited; Cash goes out and is debited
Furniture is an expense and is debited; Cash is credited
Both Furniture and Cash are debited as they are assets
questions.e: For real accounts, debit what comes in and credit what goes out. Furniture is an asset, not an expense, and a single transaction cannot be debited on both sides.

questions.s: Which of the following accounts increases with a credit entry?
questions.e: Commission received is an income, and incomes increase on the credit side. Carriage inwards is an expense, furniture an asset and drawings a reduction of capital; all increase with a debit.

questions.s: Which transaction leaves the total of the accounting equation unchanged?
o: Cash of Rs 50,000 is deposited in the bank
A bank loan of Rs 50,000 is received
A creditor is paid Rs 50,000 in cash
The owner introduces cash of Rs 50,000
questions.e: Depositing cash only moves money from one asset (cash) to another (bank). Each of the other transactions changes total assets together with liabilities or capital.

questions.s: Which transaction reduces both assets and capital?
o: Paying the electricity bill in cash
questions.e: An expense paid in cash reduces cash and reduces profit, and therefore capital. Paying a creditor reduces assets and liabilities, not capital.

questions.s: Hina starts a business with Rs 300,000 cash. She buys goods for Rs 80,000 on credit, sells half of these goods for Rs 55,000 cash, and pays Rs 50,000 to the creditor. What are her total assets now?
questions.e: Cash = 300,000 + 55,000 − 50,000 = 305,000, and unsold stock = 40,000, so assets = Rs 345,000 (capital 315,000 + creditor 30,000). Rs 385,000 forgets that half the stock has been sold.

questions.s: When a customer pays cash, which document does the business give the customer as proof of payment?
questions.e: A receipt confirms that money has been received. A statement of account only lists what the customer owes, and a purchase order is sent by a buyer to order goods.

questions.s: Which source document does the payer use to record a payment made by cheque?
questions.e: The counterfoil (stub) left in the cheque book shows the date, payee and amount of each cheque issued. A pay-in slip records money deposited into the bank, not paid out.

questions.s: A trader deposits the day's cash takings into his bank account. Which source document supports the entry?
questions.e: The pay-in (deposit) slip, stamped by the bank, is evidence of money paid into the account. A cheque counterfoil records money paid out by cheque.

questions.s: Which task belongs to book-keeping rather than to the wider work of accounting?
o: Interpreting the results for the owner
Working out ratios to judge profitability
Advising whether the business should expand
Recording daily transactions in the books
questions.e: Book-keeping is the routine recording of transactions. Accounting goes further: summarising, analysing and interpreting that record for decisions.

questions.s: A bank is deciding whether to lend money to a shopkeeper. Which information from his accounts matters most to the bank?
o: Whether he can repay the loan with interest
How many employees he has on his staff
The names of his regular customers
The brand of goods he sells most
questions.e: Lenders use accounts to judge profitability and liquidity, that is, the ability to repay. The other details may be interesting but do not show whether the loan is safe.

questions.s: Which concept requires the life of a business to be divided into equal periods, usually one year, for reporting results?
questions.e: The accounting period (periodicity) concept divides the life of the business into periods so that profit can be measured regularly. Going concern only assumes the business will continue.

questions.s: Recording transactions on the basis of verifiable evidence, such as invoices and receipts, follows the:
questions.e: Objectivity requires records to rest on evidence that others can check, not on personal opinion. Prudence is about caution in recognising profits and losses.

questions.s: A trader expects to win a court case worth Rs 200,000 and also fears losing another case worth Rs 50,000. Under the prudence concept, what should he do?
o: Provide for the Rs 50,000 loss but not record the gain
Record the gain and ignore the possible loss
Record a net gain of Rs 150,000
Record both the gain and the loss
questions.e: Prudence says anticipate no profit but provide for all likely losses. The expected gain is not yet realised, so it is not recorded, while the likely loss is provided for.

questions.s: A business takes a loan of Rs 500,000 from a bank, received by cheque and deposited. Which entry is correct?
questions.e: The bank balance (asset) rises, so Bank is debited; the loan (liability) rises, so Bank Loan is credited. Crediting Capital would wrongly treat borrowed money as the owner's investment.

questions.s: Goods are bought on credit from Raza Brothers. Which entry is correct?
questions.e: Purchases (an expense) is debited and the supplier, who gives the goods and is now owed money, is credited. Crediting Cash would be correct only for a cash purchase.

questions.s: Which pair of accounts normally have credit balances?
questions.e: Sales is an income and Creditors a liability, so both are credit balances. Purchases, Debtors, Drawings and Returns Inwards all carry debit balances.

questions.s: In a trader's trial balance, which of these items appears in the debit column?
questions.e: Discount allowed to customers is an expense (a loss of revenue), so it is a debit balance. Discount received is a gain, returns outwards reduces purchases, and a bank loan is a liability: all credits.

questions.s: A firm's capital is three times its liabilities, and its total assets are Rs 640,000. What is its capital?
questions.e: Assets = Capital + Liabilities = 3L + L = 4L, so L = 640,000 ÷ 4 = 160,000 and capital = 3 × 160,000 = Rs 480,000. Rs 160,000 is the liabilities figure.

questions.s: What is the left-hand side of a ledger account called?
questions.e: By convention the left side of a T-account is the debit (Dr) side and the right side is the credit (Cr) side. A narration is the short explanation written under a journal entry.

questions.s: The owner takes goods costing Rs 18,000 from the business for her family's use. What is the effect on the accounting equation?
o: Assets fall and liabilities rise by Rs 18,000
Assets stay the same and capital falls by Rs 18,000
Assets and capital both fall by Rs 18,000
Assets fall by Rs 18,000 and capital is unchanged
questions.e: Stock (an asset) leaves the business, and drawings reduce the owner's capital by the same amount. No outsider is owed anything, so liabilities do not change.

questions.s: Usman pays his son's school fee of Rs 25,000 from the business bank account. Which entry is correct?
questions.e: A private expense paid from business funds is a withdrawal by the owner, so Drawings is debited. Treating it as a business expense would break the business entity concept and understate profit.

questions.s: Which transaction increases total assets but leaves the owner's capital unchanged?
o: Selling goods at a profit for cash
questions.e: A credit purchase adds stock and adds an equal liability, so capital is untouched. Commission earned, extra capital and a profitable sale all raise capital as well as assets.

questions.s: Which form of the accounting equation is correct?
questions.e: Assets are financed either by the owner (capital) or by outsiders (liabilities), so Assets = Capital + Liabilities. Rearranged, Capital = Assets − Liabilities.

questions.s: Accounts are prepared on the assumption that the business will continue to operate for the foreseeable future. This is the:
questions.e: The going concern concept assumes the business is not about to close, which is why assets are not valued at break-up prices. The accounting period concept only divides its life into reporting periods.

questions.s: A business has total assets of Rs 900,000 and capital of Rs 650,000. What are its liabilities?
questions.e: Liabilities = Assets − Capital = 900,000 − 650,000 = Rs 250,000. Adding the figures gives Rs 1,550,000, which mixes up the two sides of the equation.

questions.s: Wages of Rs 8,000 are paid in cash. Which entry is correct?
questions.e: Wages are an expense, increased by a debit; cash goes out, so Cash is credited. Debiting Cash would show money coming in.

questions.s: Sana, a debtor, pays Rs 15,000 in cash to settle part of her account. Which entry is correct?
questions.e: Cash comes in (debit) and Sana, who gives the money, is credited, reducing what she owes. Crediting Sales would count the same sale twice; it was recorded when the goods were sold.

questions.s: A seller sends a buyer a document listing goods sold on credit, with quantities, prices and the total due. What is it called?
questions.e: An invoice records a credit sale and the amount the buyer owes; to the buyer it is a purchase invoice. A receipt is issued only when payment is received.

questions.s: Which of the following is a nominal account?
questions.e: Nominal accounts record expenses, losses, incomes and gains, so Interest Paid is nominal. Bank and Creditors are personal accounts and Land is a real account.

questions.s: Old furniture with a book value of Rs 20,000 is sold for exactly Rs 20,000 in cash. What is the effect on the accounting equation?
o: Assets and capital both rise by Rs 20,000
Assets fall and capital falls by Rs 20,000
One asset rises and another falls; totals are unchanged
Assets rise and liabilities rise by Rs 20,000
questions.e: Cash rises by 20,000 and furniture falls by 20,000. With no profit or loss on sale, capital and liabilities are untouched.

questions.s: A trader's capital was Rs 180,000 at the start of the year and Rs 230,000 at the end. During the year he withdrew Rs 36,000 and introduced extra capital of Rs 20,000. What was his profit?
questions.e: Profit = Closing − Opening + Drawings − New capital = 50,000 + 36,000 − 20,000 = Rs 66,000. Rs 86,000 forgets that part of the rise came from new capital, not profit.

questions.s: Nadia pays Rs 30,000 owed by her business to a supplier out of her personal savings. Which entry is made in the business's books?
questions.e: The business's debt falls (debit the supplier), and the owner has in effect put Rs 30,000 into the business, so Capital is credited. No business cash was used, so Cash is not credited.

questions.s: Which concept means that once a business values its stock by one method, it keeps using the same method year after year?
questions.e: Consistency keeps methods unchanged between periods so that results can be compared. Prudence affects how cautiously stock is valued, not whether the method stays the same.

questions.s: Which account increases on the debit side?
questions.e: Expenses, assets and drawings increase with a debit. Capital, sales (income) and creditors (liability) all increase with a credit.

questions.s: How is an increase in a liability recorded?
o: As a debit to the liability account
As a credit to the liability account
As a debit to the capital account
As a credit to the drawings account
questions.e: Liabilities, like capital and income, increase on the credit side. A debit to a liability account records a decrease, such as paying off part of a loan.

questions.s: Which of the following is a liability of a business?
questions.e: A bank overdraft is money owed to the bank, so it is a liability. Debtors, prepaid insurance and closing stock are all assets: amounts owed to, paid in advance by, or held by the business.

questions.s: Which sequence shows the usual order of the accounting cycle?
o: Ledger, journal, trial balance, final accounts
Journal, ledger, trial balance, final accounts
Journal, trial balance, ledger, final accounts
Trial balance, journal, ledger, final accounts
questions.e: Transactions are first recorded in the journal (books of original entry), posted to the ledger, balanced and listed in a trial balance, and then used to prepare the final accounts.

questions.s: Why is the journal called a book of original entry?
o: It is the final record from which accounts are prepared
It shows the balance of every account at the year end
It is used only when a business first starts trading
Transactions are first recorded in it from source documents
questions.e: Each transaction is first written in the journal, in date order, from its source document, and later posted to the ledger. Balances are found in the ledger, not in the journal.

questions.s: In a journal entry, what is the narration?
o: The ledger page number of each account
The total of the debit and credit amounts
A short explanation written below the entry
The signature of the person passing the entry
questions.e: The narration briefly explains the transaction, for example 'Being goods sold to Ali on credit'. The ledger page number goes in the folio (L.F.) column.

questions.s: A cloth merchant buys machinery for Rs 150,000 on credit from Khan Engineering. Which journal entry is correct?
questions.e: Machinery is a fixed asset, not goods for resale, so the Machinery account is debited rather than Purchases. The supplier gives credit and is credited; no cash is paid.

questions.s: Goods worth Rs 32,000 are sold to Fatima; she pays half in cash and owes the rest. Which journal entry is correct?
o: Sales Dr 32,000; Cash Cr 16,000; Fatima Cr 16,000
Cash Dr 16,000; Fatima Dr 16,000; Sales Cr 32,000
questions.e: This is a compound entry: the full sale of Rs 32,000 is credited to Sales, with Cash and Fatima each debited Rs 16,000. Recording only the cash half leaves out the credit sale.

questions.s: A business pays Asif Rs 9,500 in cash in full settlement of Rs 10,000 it owes him. Which journal entry is correct?
o: Asif Dr 10,000; Cash Cr 9,500; Discount Received Cr 500
Asif Dr 10,000; Cash Cr 9,500; Discount Allowed Cr 500
Cash Dr 9,500; Discount Received Dr 500; Asif Cr 10,000
questions.e: Asif's whole debt of Rs 10,000 is cleared (debit), cash of Rs 9,500 goes out, and the Rs 500 saved is a gain, Discount Received (credit). Discount allowed is what a business gives to its customers.

questions.s: Junaid owes the business Rs 20,000 and pays Rs 19,000 in cash in full settlement. Which statement about the journal entry is correct?
o: Discount Received is credited with Rs 1,000
Junaid is credited with Rs 19,000 only
Discount Allowed is debited with Rs 1,000
questions.e: The entry is Cash Dr 19,000; Discount Allowed Dr 1,000; Junaid Cr 20,000. The discount is a loss given to a customer, so it is a debit; Junaid is credited with the full Rs 20,000 because his debt is fully cleared.

questions.s: What does the sales book (sales day book) record?
o: All sales of goods and fixed assets
questions.e: The sales book records only credit sales of the goods the business deals in. Cash sales go in the cash book, and returns by customers go in the sales returns book.

questions.s: A cloth trader buys a computer on credit for office use. In which book is this first recorded?
questions.e: The purchases book records only credit purchases of goods for resale. A fixed asset bought on credit is recorded in the journal proper.

questions.s: What does the purchases returns book record?
o: Goods returned to suppliers that were bought on credit
Goods returned by customers to the business
Credit purchases of goods for resale
questions.e: The purchases returns (returns outwards) book lists goods sent back to suppliers, usually supported by debit notes. Returns from customers go in the sales returns book.

questions.s: Goods with a list price of Rs 50,000 are sold on credit at a trade discount of 10 %. At what amount is the sale entered in the sales book?
questions.e: Trade discount is deducted before the sale is recorded: 50,000 − 10 % = Rs 45,000. It never appears in the ledger, so the list price of Rs 50,000 is not entered.

questions.s: Goods with a list price of Rs 80,000 are sold at a trade discount of 20 %, and a cash discount of 5 % is given because the customer pays at once. How much cash is received?
questions.e: After trade discount: 80,000 × 80 % = 64,000. Cash discount: 5 % of 64,000 = 3,200, so cash received = Rs 60,800. Rs 60,000 wrongly adds the two rates (25 %) and applies them to the list price.

questions.s: How are the entries in the sales book posted to the ledger?
o: Each customer is credited; the Sales account is debited with the total
Only the total is posted, to the debit of the Sales account
Each customer is debited; the Sales account is credited with the total
Each customer is debited; the Cash account is credited with the total
questions.e: Customers become debtors, so each is debited individually; the periodic total of the book is credited to the Sales account. Cash is not involved in credit sales.

questions.s: To which side of which account is the monthly total of the purchases returns book posted?
o: Debit side of the Purchases Returns account
Credit side of the Purchases account
Credit side of the Purchases Returns account
Debit side of each supplier's account
questions.e: The total is credited to Purchases Returns (Returns Outwards). The individual suppliers are debited, entry by entry, since the business now owes them less.

questions.s: When balancing a ledger account, the debit side totals more than the credit side. What kind of balance does the account have?
questions.e: The account's balance is named after the larger side. The difference is written as 'Balance c/d' on the smaller (credit) side and brought down on the debit side.

questions.s: A cash account shows the entries below. What is the balance carried down at the end of the month?
questions.e: Debit total = 50,000 + 18,000 + 7,000 = 75,000; credit total = 22,000 + 13,500 = 35,500. Balance = 75,000 − 35,500 = Rs 39,500, a debit balance; cash can never have a credit balance.

questions.s: Ali is a supplier. During April the business bought goods from him on credit for Rs 40,000 and Rs 25,000, paid him Rs 30,000 and returned goods worth Rs 3,000 to him. There was no opening balance. What is the balance on Ali's account at the end of April?
questions.e: Credits (purchases) = 65,000; debits (payment and returns) = 33,000. Balance = Rs 32,000 credit: the business still owes Ali. Adding the returns instead of deducting them gives Rs 38,000.

questions.s: The journal entry 'Rent Dr Rs 15,000, Bank Cr Rs 15,000' is posted to the Rent account. How does it appear there?
questions.e: Rent is debited, so the entry goes on the debit side, and the name written is the other account involved: 'To Bank'. In the Bank account it appears on the credit side as 'By Rent'.

questions.s: What is the transfer of entries from the journal to the ledger accounts called?
questions.e: Posting moves each debit and credit from the journal to the right ledger account. Journalising is the first recording in the journal, and balancing finds the closing figure of an account.

questions.s: What does the folio (L.F.) column of a journal show?
o: The date on which the transaction took place
The invoice number of the source document
The ledger page of the account the entry is posted to
The total of each page of the journal
questions.e: The ledger folio gives the page number of the account in the ledger, showing that posting is done and making entries easy to trace. The date has its own column.

questions.s: What is a cash book with separate columns for cash and for bank called?
questions.e: A double column cash book has cash and bank columns on each side. A triple column cash book adds a discount column as well.

questions.s: Cash of Rs 25,000 is deposited into the business bank account. How is this recorded in a double column cash book?
o: Debit cash column and credit bank column, marked C
Debit bank column and credit cash column, marked C
Debit bank column only, with no other entry
Credit cash column and debit Capital account
questions.e: This is a contra entry: both sides are inside the cash book. Bank receives (debit bank column) and cash goes out (credit cash column); 'C' in the folio column shows no ledger posting is needed.

questions.s: Why is the cash book said to serve as a journal as well as a ledger?
o: It records every transaction of the business, cash or credit
It is prepared once a year from the trial balance
It lists the balances of all the personal accounts
It is a book of original entry and also the cash and bank accounts
questions.e: Cash transactions are first entered in the cash book (journal role), and its columns are themselves the cash and bank accounts (ledger role), so no separate cash account is kept.

questions.s: In a triple column cash book, how is the total of the discount column on the debit side posted?
o: To the credit of the Discount Allowed account
To the debit of the Discount Received account
To the debit of the Discount Allowed account
To the credit of the Cash account
questions.e: Discounts on the receipts (debit) side are allowed to customers, a loss for the business, so their total is debited to Discount Allowed. The discount column is a memorandum column, not part of the cash balance.

questions.s: In a double column cash book, which balance is impossible?
o: A credit balance in the cash column
A debit balance in the bank column
A credit balance in the bank column
A debit balance in the cash column
questions.e: A business cannot pay out more cash than it has, so the cash column always shows a debit balance or nil. A credit balance in the bank column is possible: it is an overdraft.

questions.s: A double column cash book opens with cash Rs 12,000 and bank Rs 45,000 (both debit). During the week: cash sales Rs 30,000; wages paid in cash Rs 6,000; cash deposited into the bank Rs 25,000; a creditor paid by cheque Rs 52,000. What is the closing bank balance?
questions.e: Bank = 45,000 + 25,000 (contra deposit) − 52,000 = Rs 18,000 debit. Forgetting the deposit gives a false overdraft of Rs 7,000; Rs 11,000 is the closing cash balance.

questions.s: A petty cashier works on the imprest system with a float of Rs 10,000. During the month she spends Rs 2,150 on postage, Rs 3,400 on travel and Rs 1,800 on stationery. How much does the main cashier give her to restore the float?
questions.e: Under the imprest system the cashier is reimbursed exactly what was spent: 2,150 + 3,400 + 1,800 = Rs 7,350. Rs 2,650 is the cash left in hand, not the amount needed to restore the float.

questions.s: What is the main purpose of a trial balance?
o: To work out the net profit for the year
To show the financial position of the business
To check the arithmetical accuracy of the ledger
To record transactions in date order
questions.e: A trial balance lists ledger balances; if the debit and credit totals agree, double entry has probably been carried out correctly. Profit is found in the income statement and position in the balance sheet.

questions.s: Which error will NOT stop a trial balance from agreeing?
o: A credit sale left out of the books entirely
A debit entry posted without its matching credit
An account balance added up wrongly
Rs 450 posted as Rs 540 on one side only
questions.e: If a transaction is omitted completely, neither the debit nor the credit is recorded, so the totals still agree. The other errors affect only one side and cause a difference.

questions.s: The trial balance below is complete except for the capital. What is the capital?
questions.e: Debit total = 20,000 + 140,000 + 45,000 + 90,000 + 18,000 + 12,000 = 325,000. Credits other than capital = 248,000, so capital = Rs 77,000. Rs 53,000 wrongly treats drawings as a credit.

questions.s: In which column of the trial balance does a bank overdraft appear?
o: Debit column, as it is an asset
Debit column, as it is an expense
It is shown only as a note
Credit column, as it is a liability
questions.e: An overdraft is money owed to the bank, so the bank account has a credit balance and goes in the credit column. A favourable bank balance would be a debit.

questions.s: Why is closing stock usually not listed in the trial balance?
o: It is always included in the purchases figure
It is an expense already shown under cost of sales
It is a liability that is shown separately
It has not yet been entered in any ledger account
questions.e: Closing stock is counted and valued at the year end and entered in the books only through the closing entries, so it is given as a note below the trial balance. Opening stock does appear, because it is already in the ledger.

questions.s: A credit sale of Rs 6,000 to Rehan was correctly entered in the sales book but posted to Rehan's account as Rs 600. What is the effect on the trial balance?
o: The credit total is Rs 5,400 less than the debit total
The debit total is Rs 5,400 less than the credit total
The debit total is Rs 6,600 less than the credit total
questions.e: Sales is credited with the full 6,000 through the book total, but Rehan is debited with only 600, so debits fall short by 6,000 − 600 = Rs 5,400.

questions.s: At the start of a new year, a business records its assets, liabilities and capital brought forward from last year. What is this entry called?
questions.e: The opening entry, made in the journal proper, debits the assets and credits the liabilities and capital so the new books start with the old balances. A contra entry is between cash and bank.

questions.s: A business starts the year with cash Rs 30,000, stock Rs 70,000, debtors Rs 25,000 and creditors Rs 40,000. In the opening entry, what amount is credited to Capital?
questions.e: Capital = Assets − Liabilities = (30,000 + 70,000 + 25,000) − 40,000 = Rs 85,000. Rs 125,000 forgets that creditors are also credited in the opening entry.

questions.s: Which source documents are used to write up the sales returns book?
o: Copies of credit notes issued to customers
questions.e: When customers return goods, the seller issues credit notes, and their copies are entered in the sales returns book. Debit notes sent to suppliers support the purchases returns book.

questions.s: Which posting from the sales book is made separately for each entry, rather than as a single total?
o: A debit to each customer's account
A credit to each customer's account
A credit to the Sales account for each invoice
A debit to the Cash account for each sale
questions.e: Each customer's account is debited with his own invoice so that the business knows what each debtor owes. The Sales account needs only the periodic total.

questions.s: Which kind of discount is never entered in a ledger account?
o: Discount on settlement of a debt
questions.e: Trade discount is simply deducted from the list price on the invoice, so only the net amount is recorded. Cash discounts are recorded, as Discount Allowed or Discount Received.

questions.s: A balance carried down (c/d) on the credit side of an account at the end of March appears at the start of April as:
o: a balance brought down on the credit side
a balance brought down on the debit side
a balance carried down on the debit side
a transfer to the trial balance credit column
questions.e: The balance c/d is written on the smaller side to make the totals equal, then brought down (b/d) on the opposite side. Here, a c/d on the credit side means the account has a debit balance.

questions.s: The business withdraws Rs 20,000 from its bank account for office use. Which entry is correct?
questions.e: Cash comes in and the bank balance goes down, so Cash is debited and Bank credited; it is a contra entry. Drawings would apply only if the money were taken for the owner's personal use.

questions.s: The owner withdraws Rs 20,000 from the business bank account for personal use. Which entry is correct?
questions.e: Money taken for personal use is drawings, debited; the business bank balance falls, credited. Cash Dr, Bank Cr would be correct only if the money stayed in the business as office cash.

questions.s: Goods worth Rs 60,000 are bought from Tariq, and Rs 20,000 is paid to him at once by cheque. Which journal entry is correct?
o: Purchases Dr 60,000; Bank Cr 20,000; Tariq Cr 40,000
Purchases Dr 60,000; Tariq Cr 60,000; Bank Cr 20,000
Tariq Dr 20,000; Purchases Dr 40,000; Bank Cr 60,000
questions.e: The full purchase of Rs 60,000 is debited; Rs 20,000 is paid by cheque (credit Bank) and Rs 40,000 is still owed to Tariq (credit Tariq). Debits must equal credits, which the third option breaks.

questions.s: Uninsured goods costing Rs 25,000 are destroyed by fire. Which journal entry is correct?
o: Purchases Dr, Loss by Fire Cr
Loss by Fire Dr, Purchases Cr
Loss by Fire Dr, Sales Cr
Loss by Fire Dr, Cash Cr
questions.e: The loss is a nominal account, debited; Purchases is credited at cost because those goods are no longer available for sale. No cash moves and nothing is sold.

questions.s: Goods costing Rs 40,000 are destroyed by fire, and the insurance company accepts a claim of Rs 30,000. Which journal entry is correct?
o: Insurance Co. Dr 30,000; Loss by Fire Dr 10,000; Purchases Cr 40,000
Loss by Fire Dr 40,000; Insurance Co. Cr 30,000; Purchases Cr 10,000
questions.e: Purchases is credited with the full cost of 40,000. The insurer now owes 30,000 (debit, a debtor), and the 10,000 not covered is a loss (debit).

questions.s: Goods costing Rs 2,000 are given away as free samples to promote sales. Which journal entry is correct?
questions.e: Free samples are a selling expense, so Advertisement is debited and Purchases credited at cost. Drawings applies only to goods taken for the owner's own use.

questions.s: Carriage of Rs 1,500 is paid on goods purchased. Which account is debited?
questions.e: Carriage on purchases brings goods in, so it is carriage inwards, part of the cost of goods. Carriage outwards is paid on goods sent to customers.

questions.s: Which book records the credit purchases of goods bought for resale?
questions.e: The purchases (day) book lists credit purchases of trading goods from suppliers' invoices. Cash purchases go in the cash book; credit purchases of fixed assets go in the journal proper.

questions.s: The sales book of a shop for March is shown below. Asma had no opening balance and paid nothing during March. What is the balance of Asma's account at the end of March?
questions.e: Asma is debited with each of her invoices: 18,000 + 6,500 = Rs 24,500, a debit balance because she owes the business. Rs 60,000 is the month's total, which is credited to the Sales account.

questions.s: From what is a trial balance prepared?
o: The balances of the ledger accounts at a date
The entries in the journal for one month
The final accounts of the previous year
The source documents for the period
questions.e: A trial balance is a list of all ledger balances on a particular date, debits in one column and credits in the other. The journal and documents come earlier in the cycle.

questions.s: A trial balance shows debit totals of Rs 482,000 and credit totals of Rs 470,000. A purchase of Rs 6,000 is found to have been posted twice to the debit of the Purchases account. After this is corrected, by how much will the totals still differ?
questions.e: Removing the extra 6,000 debit gives debits of 476,000 against credits of 470,000, so a difference of Rs 6,000 remains, caused by some other error. The trial balance would agree only if the whole Rs 12,000 were explained.

questions.s: In the business's ledger, what does a debit balance on a customer's account mean?
o: The business owes money to the customer
The customer has paid in advance
The customer owes money to the business
The customer has returned all the goods
questions.e: Customers are debited with sales and credited with payments and returns, so a debit balance means sales exceed payments: the customer is a debtor. An advance payment would leave a credit balance.

questions.s: Which of these accounts can show either a debit or a credit balance?
questions.e: The bank account has a debit balance when there is money in it and a credit balance when it is overdrawn. Cash cannot fall below nil, and purchases and furniture always carry debit balances.

questions.s: In a triple column cash book for June, the discount column on the debit side totals Rs 2,350 and on the credit side Rs 1,600. How are these totals posted?
o: Discount Allowed Cr 2,350; Discount Received Dr 1,600
Discount Received Dr 2,350; Discount Allowed Cr 1,600
Discount Allowed Dr 750 as a net figure
Discount Allowed Dr 2,350; Discount Received Cr 1,600
questions.e: Discounts beside receipts are allowed to customers (debit Discount Allowed); discounts beside payments are received from suppliers (credit Discount Received). The two are posted separately, never netted.

questions.s: At the year end, the Purchases account shows debit entries of Rs 48,000 and Rs 37,000 and no credit entries. How is this account closed?
o: Its balance is carried down to the next year
Its balance is transferred to the trading account
Its balance is transferred to the capital account
Its balance is shown in the balance sheet
questions.e: Purchases is a nominal account, so its Rs 85,000 balance is closed by transfer to the trading account to work out gross profit. Only real and personal accounts, such as assets and creditors, are carried down to the next year.

questions.s: Goods are sold for Rs 7,000 in cash. Which entry is correct?
questions.e: Cash comes in (debit) and the sale is an income (credit). Debtors would be debited only for a credit sale.

questions.s: A customer, Hamza, returns goods worth Rs 2,000 that he had bought on credit. Which entry is correct?
questions.e: Returns inwards reduce sales, so Sales Returns is debited; Hamza now owes less, so he is credited. Purchases Returns is for goods the business sends back to suppliers.

questions.s: Which of the following is a book of original entry?
questions.e: The cash book records cash and bank transactions for the first time, so it is a book of original entry. The ledger receives postings, and the trial balance and balance sheet are prepared later.

questions.s: To which side of which account is the total of the purchases book posted?
o: Debit side of the Purchases account
Credit side of the Purchases account
Debit side of each supplier's account
Credit side of the Cash account
questions.e: The periodic total of credit purchases is debited to the Purchases account, while each supplier is credited individually. No cash is involved.

questions.s: Insurance of Rs 7,200 is paid by cheque. Which entry is correct?
questions.e: Insurance is an expense (debit); payment by cheque reduces the bank balance (credit Bank). Crediting Cash would be right only for payment in notes and coins.

questions.s: Daniyal owes Rs 15,000 and settles his account with a cheque for Rs 14,700. How is the difference recorded?
questions.e: The business accepts Rs 300 less than it is owed, a discount allowed to a customer, which is debited. Daniyal is credited with the full Rs 15,000, closing his account.

questions.s: Rashid, a supplier, had a credit balance of Rs 22,000 on 1 May. During May goods of Rs 18,000 were bought from him on credit, and he was paid Rs 25,000 by cheque and allowed a discount of Rs 1,000. What is the balance on his account on 31 May?
questions.e: Credits = 22,000 + 18,000 = 40,000; debits = 25,000 + 1,000 = 26,000. Balance = Rs 14,000 credit, still owed to Rashid. The discount received reduces the debt, like a payment.

questions.s: Cash of Rs 10,000 is withdrawn from the bank for office use. How is it shown in a double column cash book?
o: Debit bank column and credit cash column
Debit cash column and credit Capital
Debit cash column and credit bank column
questions.e: Cash is received (debit cash column) and the bank balance falls (credit bank column). Both entries are in the cash book, so it is a contra entry.

questions.s: From the trial balance below, in which every balance except capital is given, find the capital.
Which of these errors will cause the trial balance to disagree?
o: A transaction omitted from the books entirely
Wages correctly posted but to the Rent account
A wrong amount used for both the debit and the credit
An amount posted to the debit side of one account only
questions.e: If only one side of a transaction is posted, the debits and credits no longer match. The other errors keep the two sides equal, so the trial balance still agrees.

questions.s: What is another name for the sales returns book?
questions.e: Goods returned by customers come back in, so the sales returns book is also called the returns inwards book. Returns outwards are returns to suppliers.

questions.s: Goods with a list price of Rs 36,000 are bought on credit at a trade discount of 15 %. At what amount are they entered in the purchases book?
questions.e: Trade discount = 15 % of 36,000 = 5,400, so the net amount = Rs 30,600. Only the net figure is recorded; trade discount does not enter the books.

questions.s: A cash book shows opening cash of Rs 5,000. A debtor who owes Rs 22,000 pays in cash, less a 2 % cash discount, and rent of Rs 9,000 is paid in cash. What is the closing cash balance?
questions.e: Cash received = 22,000 − 2 % = 21,560. Closing cash = 5,000 + 21,560 − 9,000 = Rs 17,560. Rs 18,000 forgets the discount of Rs 440.

questions.s: When a ledger account is balanced, on which side is the 'balance c/d' written?
o: The side with the larger total
The side with the smaller total
questions.e: The balance c/d is entered on the smaller side to make both totals equal, then brought down on the larger side to start the next period.

questions.s: How is gross profit calculated?
o: Purchases minus cost of goods sold
Net sales minus cost of goods sold
questions.e: Gross profit is found in the trading account: net sales less the cost of the goods sold. Deducting all expenses as well gives net profit.

questions.s: A trader's opening stock is Rs 40,000, purchases Rs 260,000, carriage inwards Rs 6,000, returns outwards Rs 10,000 and closing stock Rs 55,000. What is the cost of goods sold?
questions.e: Cost of goods sold = 40,000 + 260,000 + 6,000 − 10,000 − 55,000 = Rs 241,000. Rs 261,000 adds the returns outwards instead of deducting them from purchases.

questions.s: Where is carriage outwards shown in the final accounts?
o: As part of cost of goods in the trading account
As an expense in the profit and loss account
As a current liability in the balance sheet
questions.e: Carriage outwards is the cost of delivering goods to customers, a selling expense charged in the profit and loss account. Carriage inwards belongs in the trading account.

questions.s: Where is carriage inwards shown in the final accounts?
o: In the profit and loss account, as a selling expense
In the balance sheet, as a current asset
In the trading account, deducted from sales
In the trading account, added to purchases
questions.e: Carriage inwards is part of the cost of bringing goods into the business, so it is added to purchases in the trading account. Carriage outwards is a selling expense.

questions.s: A business has a gross profit of Rs 150,000. Its expenses are salaries Rs 48,000, rent Rs 24,000 and discount allowed Rs 3,000, and it received commission of Rs 7,000. What is its net profit?
questions.e: Net profit = 150,000 − (48,000 + 24,000 + 3,000) + 7,000 = Rs 82,000. Commission received is an income and is added; Rs 68,000 wrongly deducts it.

questions.s: Which of the following is capital expenditure for a trading business?
questions.e: Capital expenditure buys or improves a fixed asset that benefits several years, such as a new van. Repairs, fuel and wages keep the business running day to day and are revenue expenditure.

questions.s: Wages of Rs 15,000 are paid to workers for installing a new machine. How should this be treated?
o: Charged to the wages account as an expense
Charged to the profit and loss account as repairs
Added to the cost of the machine
questions.e: Installation costs are needed to bring the asset into use, so they are capital expenditure and form part of the machine's cost. Charging them as ordinary wages would understate assets and profit.

questions.s: The outside walls of the shop's existing building are repainted for Rs 40,000. How is this classified?
questions.e: Repainting keeps an existing asset in its present condition and does not add to its earning capacity, so it is revenue expenditure charged to profit and loss.

questions.s: Which of the following is a capital receipt?
o: Money received from cash sales of goods
Money received from selling an old delivery van
Interest received on a bank deposit
questions.e: A capital receipt comes from a non-recurring source such as selling a fixed asset, receiving a loan or new capital. Sales, commission and interest are revenue receipts.

questions.s: A business buys furniture for Rs 60,000 but wrongly records it as an office expense. What is the effect on the final accounts?
o: Profit and fixed assets are both understated
Profit and fixed assets are both overstated
Profit is overstated and fixed assets understated
Profit is understated and fixed assets overstated
questions.e: Charging capital expenditure as an expense increases expenses, so profit is too low, and the furniture is missing from the balance sheet, so assets are too low as well.

questions.s: What does a balance sheet show?
o: The profit or loss for a period
The financial position of a business at a date
All the cash received and paid in a year
The arithmetical accuracy of the ledger
questions.e: A balance sheet lists assets, liabilities and capital on a particular date. Profit for a period is shown in the income statement, and arithmetical accuracy is tested by the trial balance.

questions.s: Which of the following is a current asset?
questions.e: Prepaid rent is a benefit that will be used up within the year, so it is a current asset. Goodwill and furniture are non-current assets, and an overdraft is a current liability.

questions.s: A business has stock Rs 60,000, debtors Rs 45,000, cash Rs 15,000, creditors Rs 50,000 and outstanding expenses Rs 8,000. What is its working capital?
questions.e: Working capital = current assets − current liabilities = (60,000 + 45,000 + 15,000) − (50,000 + 8,000) = Rs 62,000. Rs 70,000 forgets that outstanding expenses are also a current liability.

questions.s: Wages of Rs 96,000 were paid during the year, and wages of Rs 8,000 were still owing at the year end. What amount is charged for wages in the income statement?
questions.e: Under the accruals concept, the year's full cost is charged: 96,000 + 8,000 = Rs 104,000. The Rs 8,000 also appears as a current liability in the balance sheet.

questions.s: A firm's year ends on 31 December. On 1 April it paid Rs 36,000 for one year's insurance. What insurance expense is charged in this year's income statement?
questions.e: The premium covers April to March; nine months (April to December) belong to this year: 36,000 × 9/12 = Rs 27,000. The remaining Rs 9,000 is prepaid and shown as a current asset.

questions.s: How is an outstanding (accrued) expense shown in the balance sheet?
questions.e: An outstanding expense is owed by the business and payable soon, so it is a current liability. A prepaid expense is the one shown as a current asset.

questions.s: How is a prepaid expense shown in the balance sheet?
questions.e: A prepayment is a service paid for but not yet received, a short-term benefit to the business, so it is a current asset.

questions.s: Commission of Rs 5,000 has been earned but not yet received at the year end. How is it treated in the final accounts?
o: Ignored until the cash is actually received
Added to commission income and shown as a current asset
Deducted from commission and shown as a liability
Added to commission and shown as a current liability
questions.e: Accrued income belongs to the year in which it was earned, so it is added to income; the amount receivable is a current asset. Waiting for the cash would break the accruals concept.

questions.s: Rent received during the year was Rs 66,000, of which Rs 6,000 relates to the next year. How is this shown in the final accounts?
questions.e: Only this year's rent, 66,000 − 6,000 = Rs 60,000, is income. The Rs 6,000 received in advance is owed back as a service to the tenant, so it is a current liability (income received in advance).

questions.s: A machine costs Rs 400,000 and is expected to last 6 years with a residual value of Rs 40,000. What is the annual depreciation by the straight-line method?
questions.e: Straight-line depreciation = (cost − residual value) ÷ life = (400,000 − 40,000) ÷ 6 = Rs 60,000 a year. Ignoring the residual value gives about Rs 66,667.

questions.s: A machine costing Rs 240,000 is bought on 1 October. Depreciation is charged at 10 % a year by the straight-line method, for the time the asset is held. The year ends on 31 December. What is the depreciation for the first year?
questions.e: Annual depreciation = 10 % of 240,000 = 24,000. The machine is held for 3 months (October to December): 24,000 × 3/12 = Rs 6,000. Rs 18,000 uses the nine months before purchase.

questions.s: How is depreciation for the year shown in the final accounts?
o: Charged in trading and added to the asset
Charged in profit and loss and deducted from the asset
Charged in profit and loss and added to liabilities
Shown only as a deduction from capital
questions.e: Depreciation is an expense in the profit and loss account, and the same amount reduces the asset's book value in the balance sheet. It is not a liability; nothing is owed to anyone.

questions.s: Debtors in the trial balance are Rs 200,000. A further Rs 5,000 is found to be irrecoverable and must be written off. At what figure are debtors shown in the balance sheet?
questions.e: The bad debt is charged to profit and loss and removed from debtors: 200,000 − 5,000 = Rs 195,000. Leaving debtors at Rs 200,000 would show money that will never be received.

questions.s: Debtors are Rs 200,000. Further bad debts of Rs 5,000 are to be written off, and a provision for doubtful debts of 5 % is to be made on the remaining debtors. At what net figure are debtors shown in the balance sheet?
questions.e: Remaining debtors = 200,000 − 5,000 = 195,000. Provision = 5 % of 195,000 = 9,750, so net debtors = Rs 185,250. Rs 185,000 wrongly works out the provision on the full Rs 200,000 before writing off the bad debt.

questions.s: The provision for doubtful debts stood at Rs 6,000 last year. This year the required provision is Rs 8,500. What amount is charged to this year's profit and loss account for the provision?
questions.e: Only the increase in the provision is charged: 8,500 − 6,000 = Rs 2,500. The old Rs 6,000 was already charged last year, so charging the full Rs 8,500 would count it twice.

questions.s: The provision for doubtful debts is reduced from Rs 10,000 to Rs 7,000. How is the change treated in the profit and loss account?
o: Rs 3,000 is debited as an expense
Rs 3,000 is credited as a gain
Rs 7,000 is debited as an expense
Rs 10,000 is credited as a gain
questions.e: A smaller provision is needed, so the excess of 10,000 − 7,000 = Rs 3,000 is written back to profit and loss as a gain. Debiting it would treat a reduction as a new cost.

questions.s: Which entry records closing stock at the year end?
o: Trading Account Dr, Closing Stock Cr
Closing Stock Dr, Trading Account Cr
questions.e: Closing stock is brought into the books as an asset (debit) and credited to the trading account, which reduces cost of goods sold. It then appears in the balance sheet as a current asset.

questions.s: How are the owner's drawings shown in the final accounts of a sole trader?
o: Charged as an expense in profit and loss
Added to capital in the balance sheet
Deducted from capital in the balance sheet
questions.e: Drawings are not a business expense; they reduce what the business owes the owner, so they are deducted from capital. Charging them to profit and loss would understate profit.

questions.s: In a sole trader's balance sheet, how is net profit for the year treated?
o: It is added to opening capital
It is deducted from opening capital
It is shown as a current asset
It is shown as a current liability
questions.e: Profit belongs to the owner, so it increases capital: opening capital + net profit − drawings = closing capital. A net loss would be deducted.

questions.s: Opening capital is Rs 500,000, net profit for the year Rs 90,000 and drawings Rs 36,000. At what figure is closing capital shown in the balance sheet?
questions.e: Closing capital = 500,000 + 90,000 − 36,000 = Rs 554,000. Rs 590,000 forgets to deduct drawings.

questions.s: Closing stock of Rs 30,000 is left out of the final accounts by mistake. What is the effect on gross profit?
o: Gross profit is overstated by Rs 30,000
Gross profit is understated by Rs 60,000
Gross profit is understated by Rs 30,000
questions.e: Closing stock is deducted in finding cost of goods sold. Leaving it out makes cost of goods sold Rs 30,000 too high, so gross profit is Rs 30,000 too low.

questions.s: This year's closing stock is overstated by Rs 12,000 and is not corrected. What is the effect on the profits of this year and next year?
o: This year's profit is understated; next year's is overstated
This year's profit is overstated; next year's is understated
Only this year's profit is affected
questions.e: Overstated closing stock lowers cost of goods sold, so this year's profit is too high. The same figure becomes next year's opening stock, raising next year's cost of goods sold and lowering its profit.

questions.s: Goods costing Rs 4,000 taken by the owner for personal use have not been recorded. How is this adjusted in the final accounts?
o: Add to purchases and deduct from drawings
Deduct from purchases and add to drawings
Add to sales and add to drawings
Charge as an expense in profit and loss
questions.e: The goods are no longer available for sale, so purchases are reduced by Rs 4,000, and they are a withdrawal by the owner, so drawings increase by Rs 4,000. Treating them as a sale would invent a profit.

questions.s: Where is discount received shown in the final accounts?
o: On the debit side of the profit and loss account
In the trading account, added to purchases
On the credit side of the profit and loss account
In the balance sheet as a current liability
questions.e: Discount received is a gain for the business, so it is credited to the profit and loss account. Discount allowed, a loss, is the one debited.

questions.s: How are returns inwards treated in the trading account?
questions.e: Returns inwards are goods sent back by customers, so they reduce sales to give net sales. Returns outwards are deducted from purchases.

questions.s: A trader sells all his goods at cost plus 25 %. His sales for the year are Rs 300,000. What is his gross profit?
questions.e: Sales = 125 % of cost, so cost = 300,000 × 100/125 = 240,000 and gross profit = Rs 60,000 (20 % of sales). Rs 75,000 wrongly takes 25 % of sales instead of 25 % of cost.

questions.s: Rent of Rs 6,000 is outstanding at the year end but is not recorded. What is the effect on the final accounts?
o: Profit is understated and liabilities are overstated
Profit is overstated and assets are overstated
Profit is unaffected but liabilities are understated
Profit is overstated and liabilities are understated
questions.e: The rent expense is too low, so profit is too high by Rs 6,000, and the amount owed is missing from current liabilities. Assets are not affected.

questions.s: Which of these items appears in the balance sheet rather than in the income statement?
questions.e: Prepaid insurance is a current asset. Depreciation, bad debts and discount allowed are expenses of the year and go in the profit and loss account.

questions.s: A draft net profit is Rs 120,000. It is then found that rent of Rs 6,000 is outstanding, insurance of Rs 2,000 is prepaid, and depreciation of Rs 10,000 has not been charged. What is the corrected net profit?
questions.e: Outstanding rent adds an expense (−6,000), prepaid insurance removes part of an expense (+2,000), and depreciation is an extra expense (−10,000): 120,000 − 6,000 + 2,000 − 10,000 = Rs 106,000.

questions.s: A machine costing Rs 200,000 is depreciated at 20 % a year by the reducing balance method. What is the depreciation for the second year?
questions.e: Year 1: 20 % of 200,000 = 40,000, leaving 160,000. Year 2: 20 % of 160,000 = Rs 32,000. Rs 40,000 is the first year's charge; each later year is worked on the reduced book value. Rs 128,000 is the book value left after year 2.

questions.s: Monthly rent is Rs 5,000. By the year end, rent of Rs 55,000 has been paid. What amount is charged for rent in the income statement for the year?
questions.e: The full year's rent, 12 × 5,000 = Rs 60,000, is charged. Only 11 months have been paid, so Rs 5,000 is outstanding and shown as a current liability.

questions.s: What period does an income statement cover?
o: A single date, such as 31 December
A period, such as the year ended 31 December
The whole life of the business
Only the last month of the year
questions.e: The income statement measures profit over a period, so it is headed 'for the year ended…'. The balance sheet shows position 'as at' a single date.

questions.s: Insurance of Rs 3,000 paid during the year relates to the next year. Which adjusting entry is made?
questions.e: The prepaid part is taken out of this year's expense (credit Insurance) and recorded as an asset (debit Prepaid Insurance). No cash moves in an adjusting entry.

questions.s: Salaries of Rs 9,000 for the last month of the year are unpaid. Which adjusting entry is made?
questions.e: The unpaid salary is added to this year's expense (debit Salaries) and recorded as a liability (credit Outstanding Salaries). Cash is credited only when payment is actually made.

questions.s: Which formula gives the cost of goods sold?
o: Opening stock + purchases + carriage inwards − closing stock
Opening stock + purchases + carriage outwards − closing stock
questions.e: Cost of goods sold is the goods available (opening stock, purchases and the cost of bringing them in) less what is left at the end. Carriage outwards is a selling expense, not a cost of the goods.

questions.s: A trader's opening stock is Rs 30,000, closing stock Rs 42,000 and cost of goods sold Rs 216,000. What were his purchases?
questions.e: Cost of goods sold = opening stock + purchases − closing stock, so purchases = 216,000 − 30,000 + 42,000 = Rs 228,000. Rs 204,000 swaps opening and closing stock.

questions.s: How is the provision for doubtful debts shown in the balance sheet?
o: Deducted from debtors under current assets
Added to creditors under current liabilities
questions.e: The provision reduces debtors to the amount expected to be collected, so it is shown as a deduction from debtors. It is an estimate of loss on assets, not an amount owed to anyone.

questions.s: Which of the following is revenue expenditure?
o: A new air conditioner for the shop
Legal fees for buying the shop
questions.e: Electricity is a running cost that benefits only the current period. The other three create or add to fixed assets, so they are capital expenditure.

questions.s: What does the trading account show?
questions.e: The trading account compares net sales with cost of goods sold to find gross profit. Net profit is found in the profit and loss account after other expenses and incomes.

questions.s: Opening stock is Rs 25,000, purchases Rs 180,000, returns outwards Rs 5,000 and closing stock Rs 30,000. What is the cost of goods sold?
questions.e: Cost of goods sold = 25,000 + (180,000 − 5,000) − 30,000 = Rs 170,000. Adding the returns gives Rs 180,000, but goods sent back to suppliers reduce purchases.

questions.s: Annual rent is Rs 48,000. Only Rs 40,000 has been paid by the year end. How much rent is outstanding?
questions.e: Outstanding rent = 48,000 − 40,000 = Rs 8,000, shown as a current liability. The full Rs 48,000 is still charged in the income statement.

questions.s: A van costs Rs 1,500,000 and has a residual value of Rs 300,000 after a useful life of 5 years. What is the annual depreciation by the straight-line method?
questions.e: Annual depreciation = (1,500,000 − 300,000) ÷ 5 = Rs 240,000. Rs 300,000 ignores the residual value.

questions.s: On 1 January a firm pays Rs 24,000 for one year's insurance. Its financial year ends on 31 March. How much insurance is prepaid at the year end?
questions.e: January to March (3 months, Rs 6,000) belongs to this year. The other 9 months, 24,000 × 9/12 = Rs 18,000, are prepaid and shown as a current asset.

questions.s: Debtors are Rs 80,000, of which Rs 2,000 is to be written off as bad. A provision for doubtful debts of 5 % of the remaining debtors is needed; the existing provision is Rs 3,000. What is the total charge to profit and loss for bad and doubtful debts?
questions.e: New provision = 5 % of 78,000 = 3,900; the increase over the old 3,000 is 900. Total charge = bad debt 2,000 + 900 = Rs 2,900. Rs 5,900 charges the whole new provision again.

questions.s: At the end of the year, to which account is a sole trader's net profit transferred?
questions.e: Net profit belongs to the owner, so it is credited to the capital account. The trading account comes earlier and finds only gross profit.

questions.s: How is rent received in advance shown in the balance sheet?
questions.e: Rent received in advance is income not yet earned; the business owes the tenant the use of the premises, so it is a current liability.

questions.s: Sales are Rs 360,000 and cost of goods sold is Rs 270,000. What is the gross profit as a percentage of sales?
questions.e: Gross profit = 360,000 − 270,000 = 90,000, and 90,000 ÷ 360,000 = 25 %. 33⅓ % is the gross profit as a percentage of cost, not of sales.

questions.s: A draft net profit is Rs 64,000. Depreciation of Rs 8,000 has been omitted, rent of Rs 3,000 paid for the next year was charged as an expense, and wages of Rs 2,500 are outstanding. What is the corrected net profit?
questions.e: Depreciation is a missing expense (−8,000); the prepaid rent was over-charged, so it is added back (+3,000); outstanding wages are a missing expense (−2,500): 64,000 − 8,000 + 3,000 − 2,500 = Rs 56,500.

questions.s: A machine is bought for Rs 300,000. Carriage to the factory costs Rs 8,000, installation Rs 12,000, and insurance for its first year of running Rs 5,000. At what cost is the machine recorded?
questions.e: Cost includes every expense needed to bring the asset into working condition: 300,000 + 8,000 + 12,000 = Rs 320,000. Insurance for running it is a yearly revenue expense, not part of its cost.

questions.s: Sales are Rs 480,000, returns inwards Rs 12,000 and cost of goods sold Rs 310,000. What is the gross profit?
questions.e: Net sales = 480,000 − 12,000 = 468,000, so gross profit = 468,000 − 310,000 = Rs 158,000. Rs 170,000 forgets to deduct the goods returned by customers.

questions.s: Which of the following is a non-current liability?
o: A bank loan repayable in five years
Creditors for goods bought last month
Wages outstanding at the year end
questions.e: Non-current liabilities fall due after more than one year, such as a five-year loan. Creditors, outstanding wages and an overdraft are payable within a year and are current liabilities.

questions.s: A draft net profit is Rs 75,000. Adjustments still to be made: commission earned but not received Rs 3,000; a bad debt of Rs 2,500 to be written off; and closing stock was undervalued by Rs 4,000. What is the corrected net profit?
questions.e: Accrued commission adds 3,000, the bad debt deducts 2,500, and raising closing stock by 4,000 lowers cost of goods sold, adding 4,000: 75,000 + 3,000 − 2,500 + 4,000 = Rs 79,500.

questions.s: Why is a bank reconciliation statement prepared?
o: To record all bank transactions for the first time
To find the profit earned on bank deposits
To correct errors in the trial balance
To explain the difference between the cash book and bank statement balances
questions.e: Timing differences and items known to only one side make the two bank balances differ; the statement reconciles them. It is not a book of entry and does not find profit.

questions.s: Cheques issued to suppliers have not yet been presented to the bank for payment. Compared with the cash book, the bank statement balance is:
questions.e: The cash book has already been credited with these cheques, but the bank has not yet paid them, so the bank still shows more money in the account.

questions.s: A reconciliation starts from the cash book (debit) balance. How are cheques deposited but not yet credited by the bank treated?
questions.e: The cash book already includes these deposits, but the bank statement does not. To reach the bank statement figure, they are deducted from the cash book balance.

questions.s: Bank charges of Rs 500 appear on the bank statement but not in the cash book. How is the cash book corrected?
o: Debit the bank column with Rs 500
Credit the bank column with Rs 500
Credit the cash column with Rs 500
No entry; it is shown only in the reconciliation
questions.e: Charges reduce the money in the bank, so the bank column is credited to bring the cash book up to date. The cash column is for notes and coins, not the bank account.

questions.s: A customer pays Rs 18,000 directly into the business's bank account, and the business learns of it only from the bank statement. How is the cash book updated?
o: Credit the bank column; debit the customer
Debit the cash column; credit Sales
Debit the bank column; credit Sales
Debit the bank column; credit the customer
questions.e: Money has come into the bank (debit bank column) and the customer owes less (credit the customer). The sale was recorded earlier, so crediting Sales would count it twice.

questions.s: The cash book shows a debit balance of Rs 48,000. Cheques issued but not presented total Rs 12,000, cheques deposited but not yet credited total Rs 7,500, and bank charges of Rs 600 have not been entered in the cash book. What balance does the bank statement show?
questions.e: Updated cash book = 48,000 − 600 = 47,400. Add unpresented cheques (+12,000) and deduct uncleared deposits (−7,500): Rs 51,900. Rs 52,500 forgets the bank charges.

questions.s: How does a favourable (positive) balance appear on the bank statement?
questions.e: To the bank, the customer's money is a liability, so a positive balance is shown as a credit. In the business's own cash book the same balance is a debit.

questions.s: A cheque of Rs 9,000 received from a customer, Shahid, and already deposited is returned dishonoured by the bank. Which entry is made in the cash book and ledger?
o: Debit Shahid; credit the bank column
Debit the bank column; credit Shahid
Debit Bad Debts; credit the bank column
questions.e: The money never reached the account, so the bank column is credited, and Shahid owes the amount again, so he is debited. It is not yet a bad debt; he may still pay.

questions.s: The cash book shows a debit balance of Rs 35,000. The bank statement reveals bank charges of Rs 400, interest credited Rs 1,200, a dividend of Rs 5,000 collected directly by the bank, and a customer's cheque of Rs 3,000 dishonoured. What is the corrected cash book balance?
questions.e: Corrected balance = 35,000 − 400 + 1,200 + 5,000 − 3,000 = Rs 37,800. Interest and the dividend increase the balance; charges and the dishonoured cheque reduce it.

questions.s: A credit purchase is left out of the books completely. What type of error is this?
questions.e: An error of omission occurs when a transaction is not recorded at all. Since neither side is entered, the trial balance still agrees.

questions.s: The purchase of furniture for office use is debited to the Purchases account. What type of error is this?
questions.e: Treating capital expenditure (furniture, an asset) as revenue expenditure (purchases of goods) breaks an accounting principle. The trial balance still agrees because the debit is in the right amount.

questions.s: A payment to Ali Raza is correctly recorded in the cash book but debited to the account of Ali Rehman, another supplier. What type of error is this?
questions.e: Posting to the wrong account of the same class, here the wrong supplier, is an error of commission. No principle is broken, and the trial balance still agrees.

questions.s: The Sales account is overcast by Rs 1,000 and the Wages account is also overcast by Rs 1,000. What are these called?
questions.e: One error cancels the other: credits are Rs 1,000 too high and debits are Rs 1,000 too high, so the trial balance still agrees. Such errors can hide each other.

questions.s: A credit sale of Rs 7,800 is entered in the sales book as Rs 8,700 and posted from there. What is the effect on the trial balance?
o: The debit side is Rs 900 higher
It still agrees, as both sides use Rs 8,700
The credit side is Rs 900 higher
The debit side is Rs 1,800 higher
questions.e: This is an error of original entry: the wrong figure is used for both the debit (customer) and the credit (Sales), so the totals agree even though both accounts are wrong by Rs 900.

questions.s: The debit total of a trial balance exceeds the credit total by Rs 2,400. How is the suspense account opened?
o: With a debit balance of Rs 2,400
With a credit balance of Rs 1,200
With a debit balance of Rs 4,800
With a credit balance of Rs 2,400
questions.e: The suspense account is placed on the shorter side to make the totals agree. Credits are short, so suspense is credited with Rs 2,400 until the errors are found.

questions.s: The sales book is undercast by Rs 1,000, and a suspense account has been opened. Which entry corrects the error?
questions.e: Undercasting the book means the Sales account got Rs 1,000 too little credit, while customers were posted correctly. Sales is credited and Suspense debited. Debtors are already right.

questions.s: A trial balance's credit total exceeds its debit total by Rs 3,600, and a suspense account is opened. It is found that discount allowed of Rs 1,800 was posted to the credit side of the Discount Allowed account. Which entry corrects this?
o: Discount Allowed Dr, Suspense Cr Rs 1,800
Suspense Dr, Discount Allowed Cr Rs 3,600
Discount Allowed Dr, Debtors Cr Rs 1,800
Discount Allowed Dr, Suspense Cr Rs 3,600
questions.e: The account needed a debit of 1,800 but got a credit of 1,800, so it must be debited twice the amount, Rs 3,600, to cancel the wrong entry and make the right one. This clears the suspense debit of 3,600.

questions.s: A cheque of Rs 6,000 received from Fahad was correctly entered in the cash book but posted to the debit of Fahad's account. Which entry corrects this, using a suspense account?
questions.e: Fahad should have been credited with 6,000 but was debited 6,000 instead. Crediting him with 12,000 removes the wrong debit and makes the right credit; the other side goes to Suspense.

questions.s: Under the straight-line method, how does the depreciation charge change from year to year?
o: It stays the same every year
It depends on the asset's market value
questions.e: The straight-line (fixed instalment) method spreads the cost minus residual value equally over the asset's life, so the charge is the same each year.

questions.s: Under the reducing balance method, how does the depreciation charge change from year to year?
o: It stays the same every year
It is zero after the first year
questions.e: A fixed percentage is applied to a book value that keeps falling, so each year's charge is smaller than the year before.

questions.s: A machine costing Rs 100,000 is depreciated at 10 % a year by the reducing balance method. What is its book value at the end of three years?
Equipment costing Rs 250,000, with no residual value, is depreciated at 10 % a year on cost by the straight-line method. What is its book value after four years?
questions.e: Annual depreciation = 10 % of 250,000 = 25,000; after four years, 100,000. Book value = 250,000 − 100,000 = Rs 150,000. Rs 100,000 is the total depreciation, not the book value.
